design_detail: Short single-author review (labelled REVIEW; seven printed pages, pp. 69-75, 58 references) by a forensic physician at the Department of Legal Medicine, University of Tsukuba, Japan. It summarizes how benzodiazepines and alcohol are metabolized, what single-dose pharmacokinetic studies found when alcohol was given with a benzodiazepine (Table 3, eight study arms), what two small studies found after long-term alcohol intake, and it tabulates 39 published fatal poisonings in which blood held both alcohol and one or more benzodiazepines (Table 4, 11 source reports, 1988-1999). No search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no appraisal of the cited studies and no pooling; Tables 1 and 3 are stated to be modified from the author's own earlier papers.
can_establish: What this author collected: that single-dose studies of alcohol with a benzodiazepine gave inconsistent pharmacokinetic results (five of eight arms unchanged, one decreased, one decreased on three measures, one increased by a mean 21%), that two small studies found faster diazepam elimination in people with long-term heavy alcohol use, and that in the published fatal poisonings he tabulated the blood alcohol was usually high while the benzodiazepine concentration was often inside or near its quoted therapeutic range.
cannot_establish: How often combining alcohol and a benzodiazepine causes death, breathing failure or any other harm (no denominator anywhere: the cases are reports selected by their authors and by this author, with no count of people who combined the two and were not harmed); whether the combination caused each tabulated death rather than the amount of benzodiazepine, the alcohol or other drugs present; the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search); or the size of any respiratory effect (the review states that high doses of ethanol and benzodiazepines synergistically depress respiration and cites three studies, but reports no respiratory measurement, no numbers and no comparison).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The review draws on: eight single-dose pharmacokinetic study arms in healthy volunteers (Table 3, p. 71, references 39-45); two studies of people with long-term heavy alcohol use (14 men with alcohol dependence, mean age 40, against 13 controls, four women and nine men, mean age 27; p. 73, reference 46) plus a rat experiment from the same report; and 39 fatal poisonings described in 11 published reports from 1988 to 1999 (Table 4, p. 72, references 49-58).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. Table 4 says it summarizes fatal poisonings from concomitant intake of alcohol and benzodiazepines reported from 1988 to the present (p. 73); its footnote a, on the largest source (Joynt 1993, 25 of the 39 rows), says only deaths due to drugs and death-drug related cases (p. 72).
sample.demographics: Of the 39 tabulated deaths, editors' count from Table 4 (p. 72): 16 women, 21 men, 2 with sex not printed; ages 25 to 70 where given, not printed in 4 rows. No information on medical history, psychiatric history, intent or circumstances is given for any case.
sample.selection_effects: Everything in Table 4 is a death selected for publication by its original authors and then selected again by this author; 25 of the 39 rows come from one Canadian forensic series of triazolam cases (Joynt 1993), so the table's predominance of triazolam reflects which series were published and chosen, not which benzodiazepine is most often involved in deaths. The review states that many of the reports involve triazolam probably because triazolam has a lower therapeutic concentration (2-20 ng/mL) than other benzodiazepines (p. 73). The pharmacokinetic studies are single doses in healthy volunteers; the chronic-alcohol evidence is two studies from one group in 1975.

exposure.measurement: In the cited pharmacokinetic studies, measured doses given under study conditions with blood sampling (Table 3, p. 71). In the fatal poisonings, post-mortem blood concentrations of ethanol (mg/mL) and of benzodiazepines (ng/mL) as reported by the source papers (Table 4, p. 72); amounts taken, timing and route are not given for any death.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as the conditions of the cited studies, never as guidance. Table 3 (p. 71): alprazolam 0.5 mg and 2 mg oral with ethanol 0.8 g/kg; brotizolam 0.25 mg oral with ethanol 24 g; diazepam 5 mg oral with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg oral with 0.8 g/kg (ethanol 3 hours after the diazepam); diazepam 10 mg oral with 0.8 g/kg; diazepam 10 mg oral with an intravenous ethanol infusion to a target blood concentration of 0.5 g/L; triazolam 0.5 mg oral with 25 g; triazolam 0.5 mg oral with an ethanol loading regimen (7.5 hours of oral ethanol beforehand to hold breath concentrations of 800-950 mg/L). Chronic-alcohol study: diazepam 10 mg intravenously (p. 73); rats given 15% ethanol in drinking water for 3 weeks. Post-mortem concentrations in Table 4 (p. 72): ethanol 0.1 to 3.2 mg/mL (editors' calculation from the 39 rows: median 1.7; 8 rows below 1.0 and 6 at or below 0.5); triazolam 5 to 300 ng/mL where numeric (editors' calculation: 32 of 39 rows name triazolam, median 40 ng/mL).
exposure.polysubstance: In the fatal poisonings, common and not separated: editors' count from Table 4 (p. 72) gives 14 of the 39 deaths with more than one benzodiazepine (counting diazepam with its metabolite nordiazepam, and flurazepam with 7-aminoflurazepam, as one drug) and 10 rows with unspecified others besides. One tabulated case is a fatal overdose of tramadol with alprazolam (Michaud et al. 1999, reference 57). The review states that fatal poisoning appears to occur more often with ethanol and multiple benzodiazepines than with ethanol and a single benzodiazepine, while adding that an excess total amount of benzodiazepines must also be considered (p. 73); it gives no count for this statement. In the volunteer studies only the two study drugs were given.

comparison.controls: None of the author's own. The cited single-dose studies compared a benzodiazepine with and without alcohol within healthy volunteers; the chronic-alcohol study compared 14 men with alcohol dependence against 13 controls (p. 73). Table 4 has no comparison group: no deaths from benzodiazepines without alcohol, from alcohol alone, or non-fatal cases are tabulated.
comparison.matching: In the chronic-alcohol study, none: the groups differ in sex composition (all men against four women and nine men) and in mean age (40 against 27) as printed on p. 73.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: For every tabulated death: tolerance, regular benzodiazepine or alcohol use, prescriptions held, intent, health, and the time between taking the drugs and dying.

outcomes.instruments: Pharmacokinetic parameters in the cited studies (Cmax, tmax, t1/2, metabolic clearance, AUC, plasma concentration; Table 3, p. 71). Post-mortem blood ethanol and benzodiazepine concentrations in the fatal cases, against therapeutic ranges quoted in the Table 4 footnote from one source (reference 55): triazolam 2-20, temazepam 20-800, diazepam 125-250 (anxiolytic), 200-500 (anticonvulsive), 1000-1500 (antieclamptic), nordiazepam 200-800, bromazepam 80-200, alprazolam 5-20, flurazepam 5-10, oxazepam 200-2000 ng/mL (p. 72).
outcomes.validity_norms: The therapeutic ranges in Table 4 come from a single compilation and are applied to post-mortem blood; the review does not discuss post-mortem redistribution, how post-mortem concentrations relate to concentrations in life, or how the ranges were derived. The classification of benzodiazepines as short, medium and long acting in Table 1 (p. 70) rests on half-life bands (1-5, 6-20 and over 21 hours) and marks the main CYP as not determined for 12 of the 24 listed drugs.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is operationalized only as a death certified by the source papers as a poisoning in which both substances were found. No clinical sign, no breathing measurement and no severity scale appears anywhere in the review.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: the review reports no statistical test, no p-value and no interval of its own.

analysis.effect_sizes: The review reports no effect size of its own. As cited: Table 3 (p. 71) gives, for acute ethanol with a single benzodiazepine dose, five arms unchanged (alprazolam plasma concentration; diazepam 5 mg Cmax, tmax, t1/2 and AUC; diazepam 10 mg plasma concentration with ethanol 3 hours later; diazepam 10 mg Cmax, tmax and AUC with an ethanol infusion; triazolam Cmax, tmax, t1/2 and CL), one decreased (brotizolam Cmax, t1/2 and CL), one decreased (diazepam 10 mg plasma concentration) and one increased (triazolam AUC, mean 21%). Chronic alcohol (p. 73): significantly lower diazepam concentrations in 14 men with alcohol dependence than in 13 controls after 10 mg intravenously, with more rapid elimination during their alcohol-free period; no effect size, interval or p-value is printed. Fatal cases (Table 4, p. 72), editors' calculations from the 39 rows: ethanol median 1.7 mg/mL (range 0.1 to 3.2), 17 rows at or above 2.0 and 6 at or below 0.5; triazolam named in 32 rows, 13 of them at or below 20 ng/mL (the top of the quoted therapeutic range) including traces, and 19 above it; in the 19 rows where triazolam is the only substance listed the median ethanol was 1.9 mg/mL and 6 of those 19 had triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL.
analysis.covariates: None; no analysis of the tabulated cases is performed beyond listing them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A narrative review; no protocol or registration applies and none is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 1 and 3 are stated to be modified from the author's own earlier work (Tanaka and Misawa, 1998; reference 3 for Table 3, p. 71). The pharmacodynamic claim that matters most for readers, synergistic respiratory depression, is asserted in one sentence with three citations (p. 71) and is supported by no data, no numbers and no table anywhere in the review, while the pharmacokinetic evidence, which mostly shows no change, fills a table.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Collected evidence, not new data: single doses of alcohol with a benzodiazepine changed benzodiazepine blood concentrations inconsistently across eight study arms (most unchanged); two small 1975 studies found faster diazepam elimination after long-term heavy alcohol use, attributed to CYP2E1 induction; and in 39 published fatal poisonings both substances were present, with blood alcohol usually high (editors' median 1.7 mg/mL) and the benzodiazepine often at or near a quoted therapeutic concentration, mostly triazolam, mostly from one Canadian series.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says acute alcohol with benzodiazepines is responsible for several toxicological interactions that can have significant clinical implications, that in general metabolism is delayed although some reports suggest otherwise, and that fatal poisoning involving coadministration, especially of triazolam, continues to be a serious problem (p. 69). Gaps: (1) in general metabolism is delayed does not match the author's own Table 3, where five of eight arms are unchanged, one is increased and two decreased; (2) the clinically important statement that high doses of ethanol and benzodiazepines synergistically depress respiration (p. 71) is not supported by any datum in the review, so a reader cannot see in whom, at what amounts or how much breathing was depressed; (3) continues to be a serious problem rests on 39 published deaths without any denominator, and the dominance of triazolam follows from one source series of 25 cases; (4) whether the combination rather than the benzodiazepine amount caused each death is left open by the author's own remark that an excess total amount of benzodiazepines must also be considered (p. 73); (5) nothing in the review says how commonly people who combine alcohol and benzodiazepines come to harm.

timeline.event: Sellers and Busto reviewed alcohol-benzodiazepine interactions published 1973-1980 and, as this review reports, observed that benzodiazepine concentrations are usually elevated when a single dose of each is given together (p. 71, reference 2).
Tanaka and Misawa's own update of acute alcohol with single benzodiazepine doses, from which Table 3 is modified (p. 71, reference 3).

Finnish post-mortem series comparing blood alcohol in fatal poisonings with and without a drug, including temazepam, with a denominator of 1006 deaths; the median blood alcohol was 0.8 lower in the alcohol-temazepam deaths than in the 615 alcohol-only deaths

replication.where_it_stands: Within the sources read for this library, the pharmacokinetic picture is unchanged: single doses of alcohol with a benzodiazepine do not reliably change benzodiazepine concentrations, and the concern is pharmacodynamic. The quantified post-mortem evidence read here is Koski et al. (2003) from Finland, which has a denominator; this review has none. No study with a count of people who combined the two and came to no harm was among the sources read, so this card does not state that none exists.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author at the Department of Legal Medicine, Institute of Community Medicine, University of Tsukuba, Japan (p. 69). Two of the four tables are modified from his own earlier publications. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the question people ask (what does alcohol with a benzodiazepine do to breathing and sedation, and how risky is it): controlled human laboratory work measuring ventilation, oxygen saturation and sedation with each drug alone and together, in people with and without tolerance; and, for the fatal risk, a population study with a denominator, counting deaths and non-fatal emergencies among people known to have taken both (for example from dispensing or cohort records) against those taking either alone, with post-mortem concentrations and all other drugs recorded.

domains.note: No databases, dates, search terms or inclusion criteria; Table 4 says only that it covers reports from 1988 to the present, and how those 11 reports were found is not stated.

No appraisal at all. The single-dose studies differ in dose, timing and ethanol regimen, which the review notes only as contradictory reports attributed to multiple factors (p. 73); the case reports are listed without any assessment of how cause of death was determined.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Tables 1 and 3 are modified from the author's own earlier papers (references 3 and, for Table 1, unattributed); the fatal cases are all other groups' reports.

The mechanism sections are labelled as mechanism, but the respiratory-depression sentence (p. 71) and the abstract's in general metabolism is delayed are stated as fact while the review's own Table 3 shows mostly unchanged results.

domains.domain: Balance of harms evidence: deaths are tabulated, non-fatal and no-harm outcomes are absent
domains.note: Only fatal cases appear. Nothing counts people who combined the two without harm, and no non-fatal clinical series, emergency-department data or survey is cited, so the review cannot show how often harm follows.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The editors' narrative-review checklist applies (METHODS 5.3; no validated instrument for narrative reviews), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. This is a short unsystematic review whose case table is a convenience collection dominated by one source series, with no denominator and no appraisal. It may be cited for: the inconsistency of the single-dose pharmacokinetic findings as tabulated (with the study conditions attached), the report of faster diazepam elimination after long-term heavy alcohol intake in two 1975 studies, the therapeutic ranges it quotes as quoted from one compilation, and the fact that in published fatal poisonings the benzodiazepine concentration was often inside or near the therapeutic range while blood alcohol was usually high, said as a description of selected published cases. It may not be cited for: any rate or probability of death or harm from combining alcohol with a benzodiazepine; for triazolam being more dangerous than other benzodiazepines; for the size of any respiratory effect; or for a causal statement that the combination killed the people in Table 4.

key_findings.finding: Of eight study arms of a single benzodiazepine dose with acute alcohol, five showed no change in the benzodiazepine's pharmacokinetics (alprazolam 0.5 and 2 mg plasma concentration with ethanol 0.8 g/kg; diazepam 5 mg with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg taken 3 hours later; diazepam 10 mg with an ethanol infusion; triazolam 0.5 mg with 25 g), one a decrease (brotizolam 0.25 mg with 24 g: Cmax, t1/2 and clearance), one a decrease in plasma concentration (diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg) and one an increase in AUC of mean 21% (triazolam 0.5 mg with an ethanol loading regimen).
key_findings.note: Doses are the study conditions as printed. The table is stated to be modified from Tanaka and Misawa (1998).

key_findings.finding: The review states that clinically, high doses of ethanol and benzodiazepines synergistically depress respiration, citing three studies; no respiratory measurement, number, dose-response or comparison is reported anywhere in the review for this statement.
key_findings.locator: The Interaction of Acute Ethyl Alcohol Intake and Benzodiazepines, last paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: The three cited references (40, 42, 45) are the brotizolam, diazepam-adinazolam and triazolam studies in Table 3, which the table describes by pharmacokinetic parameters only.

key_findings.finding: After 10 mg diazepam intravenously, concentrations were significantly lower in 14 men with long-term heavy alcohol use (mean age 40) than in 13 controls (four women and nine men, mean age 27), with faster elimination during the alcohol-free period; a rat experiment (15% ethanol in drinking water for 3 weeks) gave similar results. No effect size, interval or p-value is printed.
key_findings.locator: The Interaction of Chronic Alcohol Intake and Benzodiazepines, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Attributed to induction of CYP2E1 so that benzodiazepines metabolized by demethylation and hydroxylation show increased clearance; the two human studies are from one group in 1975 (references 46 and 47).

key_findings.finding: Table 4 lists 39 fatal poisonings from 11 published reports (1988-1999) in which blood held both alcohol and one or more benzodiazepines. Editors' count from the table: 25 of the 39 rows come from a single Canadian forensic series (Joynt 1993); 32 rows name triazolam; 14 involved more than one benzodiazepine and 10 more list unspecified others; 16 women, 21 men, sex not printed in 2.
In those 39 deaths, blood ethanol ranged from 0.1 to 3.2 mg/mL (editors' calculation: median 1.7; 17 rows at or above 2.0; 8 rows below 1.0 and 6 at or below 0.5 mg/mL).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed rows; the review itself gives no summary of the ethanol concentrations.

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine concentrations in those deaths were frequently inside or near the therapeutic ranges the table quotes: of the 32 rows naming triazolam, 13 were at or below 20 ng/mL (the top of the quoted range of 2-20), including traces, and 19 above it; in the 19 rows where triazolam is the only substance listed, 6 had triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL and the median ethanol was 1.9 mg/mL.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and its footnote (therapeutic levels quoted from reference 55)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed rows. The quoted ranges come from one compilation and are applied to post-mortem blood; post-mortem redistribution is not discussed in the review.

key_findings.finding: The review states that fatal poisoning, suicidal and non-suicidal, appears to occur more often when ethanol is taken with multiple benzodiazepines than with ethanol and a single benzodiazepine, while adding that an excess total amount of benzodiazepines must also be considered; no count or comparison supports this.

The review attributes the predominance of triazolam in the reports to triazolam having a lower therapeutic concentration (2-20 ng/mL) than other benzodiazepines, not to a comparison of risk between benzodiazepines.

Mechanism as described: benzodiazepines oxidized by CYP3A4 (and diazepam also by CYP2C19) can have their metabolism competitively inhibited after significant alcohol intake, whereas lorazepam, lormetazepam, oxazepam and temazepam are mainly conjugated (glucuronidation) and are not affected in this way; benzodiazepine metabolism is not catalysed by CYP2E1, the enzyme involved in alcohol metabolism.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Metabolism of Benzodiazepines, last paragraph; The Interaction of Acute Ethyl Alcohol Intake and Benzodiazepines, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Of 24 benzodiazepines listed in Table 1, the main CYP is given as not determined for 12 (including etizolam), and three (lorazepam, lormetazepam, oxazepam) are listed with glucuronidation and no CYP.
key_findings.note: Relevant where a claim would otherwise generalize an alcohol interaction from one benzodiazepine to all.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that in general metabolism of these drugs is delayed when combined with acute alcohol ingestion although some reports suggest otherwise, but the review's own Table 3 shows five of eight arms unchanged, one increased (triazolam AUC, mean 21%) and two decreased; a delay of metabolism would be expected to raise, not lower, benzodiazepine concentrations, and two of the three changed arms are decreases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's summary is not supported by the table it summarizes, and the direction of the effect is stated inconsistently. A claim should quote the table, not the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The clinically important statement that high doses of ethanol and benzodiazepines synergistically depress respiration (p. 71) is supported only by three references whose findings the review tabulates as pharmacokinetic parameters; no respiratory outcome, number or threshold for high doses appears anywhere in the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for the existence, size or dose threshold of respiratory synergy; the primary studies would have to be read.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 an orphan 48 is printed in the Age/Sex column on its own line, directly under the first Joynt row (25/F, 1.60, triazolam 10) and above a row whose age is printed as a dash with sex M; the orphan line carries no ethanol value and no benzodiazepine value. Checked on a 300-dpi crop.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typesetting fault of unknown origin: 48 may be a lost age for the row below (printed with a dash for age) or a stray figure. The editors' count of 39 deaths excludes this line, since it holds no data; if it is a lost age, the number of deaths is unchanged and one more age is known. A second reader should check it against the source series (Joynt, 1993).

reporting_issues.issue: Case 5's source (Joynt 1993) is cited in the table footnote as covering only death due to drugs and death-drug related cases, but no definition of either category, and no information on which deaths from that series were left out, is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection within the largest source series is unknown, so the distribution of concentrations in the table cannot be read as the distribution in that series.

reporting_issues.issue: The therapeutic ranges in the Table 4 footnote are cited to reference 55 (Uemura and Komura, a two-page case report in a forensic pathology journal), not to a pharmacological compilation, and are applied to post-mortem blood without discussion of post-mortem redistribution.
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements that a death occurred at a therapeutic concentration rest on ranges of uncertain provenance measured in a different setting from the one in which they were defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The chronic-alcohol comparison (14 men with alcohol dependence, mean age 40, against 13 controls, mean age 27, four of them women) is reported as significant without any effect size, interval, p-value or adjustment for the age and sex differences printed in the same sentence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and the reliability of the faster-elimination finding cannot be judged from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 51 (Wodak and Pedersen) is listed in Table 4 as a death from combined alcohol and benzodiazepine poisoning in a non-medical detoxification unit, with no age or sex printed, and the review does not say that this case occurred during alcohol withdrawal treatment, a setting unlike the others in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader counting comparable cases would need to exclude or flag it; the table treats all 39 rows alike.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, Clinical Toxicology 40(1):69-75, 2002; the copy carries a library download stamp), pp. 69-75, all 7 pages; Tables 1-4 and Figure 1 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, and every number taken from Table 3 (p. 71) and Table 4 (p. 72) read off the rendered page; no supplement.
